extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of literary travel/nature essays; students of 19th-century American prose
extracted.subtask_description: Composing episodic, journal-like travel or nature essays that combine close observation, anecdote, and personal reflection in a lyrical, descriptive prose voice. Typically dated entries and scene-based vignettes that move between particulars of place and broader philosophical or national reflections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dated, episodic journal structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize material as dated entries and short scene-vignettes (dates and locations head many passages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This text is arranged as discrete entries with date/location stamps (e.g., 'April 26.', 'NEW YORK, May 24, '79.', 'PHILADELPHIA, Aug. 26.'), suggesting a rhythm of brief, time-anchored observations rather than a continuous long-form narrative. Use headings or dates to mark shifts of scene and time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid multisensory description
rubrics_metrics.description: Evoke place through detailed sensory impressions—sight, sound, smell, touch, and motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'At sunrise, the pure clear sound of the meadow lark.' 'How the smoke crawls along, flat to the ground... I like its acrid smell--whiffs just reaching me--welcomer than French perfume.' 'The greenish-tawny, darkly transparent waters, plunging with velocity... with patches of milk-white foam.' Favor concrete, sensory specifics over abstract labels; layer multiple senses to create presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalogue concrete natural and human particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Record specific species, plants, weather, and human details rather than generic references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer lists birds ('meadow-lark', 'robin', 'wood-thrush', 'king-bird, cuckoo, warblers'), flowers ('arbutus, blue liverwort, anemone, bloodroot'), and exact human roles and items (park policeman C. C., 'Vanderbilt' steamer, 'City of Brussels'). Precise naming grounds the prose and gives authority to observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interweave short human anecdotes and vignettes
rubrics_metrics.description: Insert compact stories of people and incidents to humanize landscapes and provide narrative interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Meeting a Hermit' vignette, 'Walter Dumont and his medal' hero anecdote, and the description of the boys aboard the Minnesota. Use brief, character-focused episodes to punctuate descriptive passages and to show human responses to place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend direct personal voice with philosophical reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Move from local observation to broader, often philosophical or national reflections in a personal, first-person voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passages shift from concrete scenes to reflective claims: e.g., 'I have found the law of my own poems' and the undeivered speech about the prairies linking landscape to national character. Use the narrator's viewpoint to connect the particular to general ideas or cultural commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ rhythmic, varied, and often poetic sentence forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use long periodic sentences, lists, repetition, hyphenation and musical phrasing to create cadence and emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman's prose here uses long, rolling sentences and deliberate repetitions ('rocks, rocks, rocks'), parenthetical asides, and enumerations ('the mare and pig' style tow-list). Favor syntactic variety and musicality to match the intensity of sensory material and to sustain lyrical momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show authorial preference and candid appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: Make taste and preference explicit—state what the narrator likes or dislikes about scenes, people, and customs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator frequently comments, 'I like both sight and sound,' 'I like to watch,' and offers judgments ('they are ill at ease... far from happy'). Direct, candid appraisal helps establish voice and ethical stance; use it sparingly to guide reader interpretation.
